Issued at 255 AM EDT Wed Oct 28 2026

This Morning through Friday Night...

High clouds continue to stream across the region this morning in 
association with a subtle H5 shortwave moving across Indiana. As 
this wave ejects to the NE, drier air and clearing skies will advect 
in from the mid-Miss. Valley later today, with mostly sunny skies 
expected for all by early afternoon. While patchy morning fog has 
been a common occurrence recently, would expect the more well-mixed 
boundary layer to keep fog development at a minimum this morning, 
but some very isolated fog banks can't be ruled out in the deepest 
river valleys.

Otherwise, today should be another unseasonably warm day with highs 
reaching the mid-to-upper 70s. Tonight, clear skies should allow for 
the sheltered river valleys to decouple, with temperatures dropping 
quickly after sunset. While some of the HREF members show patchy fog 
developing Thursday morning, increasing winds atop the boundary 
layer may keep fog to a the deepest valleys once again, and the REFS 
is less bullish on fog development. For now, we'll leave fog out of 
tonight's forecast, with lows expected to range from near 40 in the 
coldest valleys to near 50 in urban/well-mixed locations.

Thursday and Friday will see fairly similar temperatures with highs 
in the mid-to-upper 70s to near 80 and lows mainly in the 40s. A 
weak cold front will try to move through the area Thursday night; 
however, building ridging aloft should cause the system to stall out 
and dissipate early Friday. Dry weather will continue likewise, 
though clouds should steadily increase through the day on Friday. 
Increasing clouds and mid-/upper-level moisture should lead to 
milder low temperatures Friday night.

Saturday through Sunday Night...

As we head into the weekend, a shortwave trough associated with the 
remnants of TC Vance are expected to move across the southern Plains 
and eject toward the Ohio Valley. Moisture will increase from the SW 
ahead of this disturbance, with a plume of 1.25"+ PW values moving 
into the area Saturday night. Confidence has been increasing that 
the daytime hours on Saturday will remain dry, with now 80-90% of 
ensemble members keeping the area rain free through 00Z Sunday. 

There is still quite a bit of uncertainty in the impacts from the 
weekend system, as the 00Z (10/28) ECMWF run now keeps the entire 
area dry through the weekend. With this being said, 85-95% of 
ensemble members do have measurable precipitation at some point 
Saturday night through Sunday, so there's still better odds than not 
that we'll see some rain this weekend. However, we'll have to see if 
this drier outlier becomes a trend over the next several runs. High 
temperatures should cool a bit over the weekend thanks to the extra 
clouds and moisture, particularly on Sunday, though we should still 
be above normal for the end of October. Low temperatures will be 
mild in the 50s, well above normal for this time of year.

Early-to-Mid Next Week...

A more active weather pattern is expected next week, with a lot of 
lingering uncertainty in the details at this time. The source of 
much of the uncertainty is a fairly complex synoptic pattern across 
North America. Sunday into Monday, troughing over the Pacific NW 
will get nudged to the east by an approaching Gulf of Alaska 
cyclone. As this trough moves east of the Rockies, the subtropical 
and polar stream waves are expected to come out of phase, resulting 
in the development of a cutoff low over the center of the CONUS 
early-to-mid next week. The low should meander across the Plains 
until another polar stream wave picks it up later in the week, at 
which point it is expected to move into the eastern US.

In the vicinity and ahead of this disturbance, increasing SW flow 
should bring a warm, moist air mass off of the Gulf, setting up the 
potential for several rounds of showers and storms. Timing and 
positioning of where this sets up is still quite variable between 
medium range guidance members, so we'll have to see some convergence 
in model solutions before we can have too much confidence. General 
signals point to continued mild temperatures until the upper low/sfc 
cold front passes, with cooling temperatures later next week.
